query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior in the HfNbTaTiZr alloy arises from internal residual stresses generated by local thermal expansion mismatch. In the as‐cast state, slight segregation and the formation of microstructural heterogeneities (such as incipient dual BCC phases or nanoscale precipitates rich in elements like Ta or Zr) produce regions with different thermal expansion coefficients. When the alloy is heated (or cooled), these mismatches lead to internal thermal stresses that alter dislocation dynamics and effective elastic moduli, thereby unifying the seemingly disparate observations from high‐temperature creep, cold rolling, elastic measurements, aging hardening, and thermal expansion effects.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy exhibiting minor compositional segregation and microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., dual BCC regions or early precipitate formation at grain boundaries).
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled homogenization treatment (high-temperature annealing designed to eliminate or minimize local compositional variations and thus thermal expansion mismatches) and compare its mechanical and thermoelastic behavior to that of the as‐cast alloy.
generation.conditions: Conduct tensile and creep tests as well as thermal expansion and elastic modulus measurements over a temperature range from near room temperature (∼293 K) up to high temperatures (600 °C to 1250 °C) under an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation effects. Use identical processing and testing strain rates in both as‐cast and homogenized (annealed) samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional heterogeneities and microphase segregation result in regions with differing thermal expansion coefficients, creating interfacial residual stresses that alter dislocation mobility and elastic strain responses.
generation.mechanism: Differential thermal expansion at microstructural interfaces induces internal residual stresses which modulate dislocation activation (thereby affecting creep and strain hardening) and modify the measured elastic moduli. This mechanism ties together the deviations in stress–strain behavior and thermal expansion data observed across different processing and test conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as‐cast alloy, the homogenized (annealed) sample—with minimized thermal expansion mismatches—will show less pronounced residual stress effects: its tensile yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures will be reduced or normalized, and its elastic moduli will vary more conventionally with temperature. In other words, the anomalous plateau or unexpected hardening behavior will be diminished relative to the as-cast baseline.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy state, which exhibits high-temperature tensile creep at 1250 °C, enhanced hardening after aging at 600–800 °C, nonstandard elastic moduli variation between 293 and 1100 K, and thermal expansion behavior that can induce additional internal stresses.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to dominate in the temperature regime where thermal expansion mismatch is significant (roughly from 600 °C up to 1250 °C) and in microstructures where even slight segregation leads to local variance in expansion behavior. Outside these conditions (for example, in fully homogenized or compositionally uniform alloys), the effect should be markedly reduced.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of the thermal expansion mismatch relative to other factors (e.g., intrinsic lattice distortion, oxidation, or other defect mechanisms) remains uncertain. The precise magnitude of residual stresses and their influence on dislocation mobility must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set in the as‐cast condition (with inherent microsegregation) and another set subjected to high-temperature, long-duration annealing to achieve chemical homogenization. Perform identical thermal expansion, elastic modulus, and high-temperature tensile/creep tests (from 600 °C to 1250 °C) on both sets.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and creep rates under controlled strain/stress conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized (annealed) samples exhibit stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior similar to the as‐cast samples (i.e., the anomalous hardening, yield strength plateaus, and elastic moduli trends remain unchanged), then the hypothesis that internal residual stresses from thermal expansion mismatch govern the behavior is falsified.

Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived from the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system has been performed. It has been shown that ductility is significantly reduced by simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy, which leads to reduction of the BCC1 phase content. These elements segregate during solidifying. Because of the miscibility gap in the Ta-Zr equilibrium phase diagram two BCC phases are found after cooling to room temperature. Clear correlation between the BCC1 phase content and the total elongation to failure of the alloy was found. Precipitation of Ta rich precipitates on grain boundaries reduces the elongation to almost zero values. No correlation was found between the tensile mechanical properties and microstructure related parameters in investigated set of alloys. The 5 element HEA alloy exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation. 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength to various extent. Some of them are ductile (NbTaTiZr, NbTaTi, NbTiZr) but some of them are brittle (TaTiZr, Nb1.5TaTiZr0.5, Nb0.5TaTiZr1.5) depending on microstructure.
